title: The old houses
intro: Antoine's, Galatoire's, Arnaud's, Commander's Palace and the other dining rooms that made New Orleans a restaurant city. Each house kept dishes that the rest of the country later learned from.

entries.title: Oysters Rockefeller
entries.summary: Oysters on the half shell under a green sauce of puréed herbs and greens, butter and breadcrumbs, baked or glazed until bubbling. Created at Antoine's in 1889, or 1899 by some accounts, it has a secret recipe; every other kitchen makes its own version.
entries.guest: Oysters Rockefeller are baked oysters on the half shell under a rich green herb sauce with butter and breadcrumbs. The dish was first made at Antoine's, in the French Quarter.

paras: Oysters Rockefeller is a dish of oysters on the half shell, opened and served in the deeper of their two shells, each covered with a green sauce and baked, or browned under fierce heat from above, until it bubbles. The sauce is a purée of green herbs and leaves cooked down in butter and bound with breadcrumbs, often lifted with an anise liqueur. Guests everywhere know the name, so every cook and server should be able to describe it and tell its story.
It also teaches the difference between a house original and a style. The original belongs to Antoine's; everything else called Oysters Rockefeller is another kitchen's version.

A common version starts with the greens. Green onions, celery and parsley, with spinach or watercress in many kitchens, are softened in butter, then puréed with fresh breadcrumbs, more butter, hot sauce, salt and a splash of Herbsaint (ERB-sant), the New Orleans anise liqueur, or Pernod, its French cousin, for a faint liquorice note. As a guide, use about 225 g (8 oz) of butter to 450 g (1 lb) of greens and herbs, with 60 g (2 oz) of breadcrumbs for two dozen oysters. Chill the sauce firm so it can be spooned or piped neatly.

Spread a baking tray or the plates with rock salt, the coarse salt sold for ice cream makers, and warm it in the oven. The salt is a bed, not a seasoning: it steadies the round shells so they sit level and keep their juices, and it holds the heat. Nest the shucked oysters, each in its deep shell, in the salt, and cover each to the rim with 15 to 30 ml (1 to 2 tbsp) of sauce.

Bake in a very hot oven, 230 to 260°C (446 to 500°F), for 5 to 10 minutes, the shorter time at the hotter end, or finish under a hot salamander, the kitchen's overhead grill (broiler), set far enough away that the sauce heats through before it browns. It is ready when the sauce bubbles at the edges and the frilled edge of the oyster, the mantle, has just begun to curl. Serve it at once, on its salt.

Pooling butter and a sliding sauce mean the sauce went on warm or had too few crumbs to bind it: chill it firm. A dull olive colour comes from greens cooked too long or a sauce held warm for hours. A watery plate means wet oysters or spinach that was not squeezed dry. A scorched top over a cold oyster means the salamander was too close. And an oyster left in the heat after its edges curl shrinks into a tough button.

Antoine's, opened in 1840 by Antoine Alciatore, credits the dish to his son, Jules. It is usually dated 1889, though some histories, 64 Parishes among them, give 1899, and no record settles it. The story usually told is that Jules wanted a local stand-in for snails, which had grown scarce, and turned to Gulf oysters. He named it for John D. Rockefeller, the oil magnate and one of the richest men in America, because the sauce was so rich. Jules kept the recipe within his kitchen, and the house still does not publish it. Antoine's has said its sauce holds no spinach, the very green most copies reach for.

Tell the story, not the secret: created at Antoine's by Jules Alciatore, in 1889 by most accounts, named for John D. Rockefeller for its richness, and never published. If a guest asks what is in the green sauce, describe the style, herbs and greens, butter, breadcrumbs and usually a touch of anise, and never claim to know Antoine's recipe or call another kitchen's version the original. Warn the guest that the rock salt and shells are very hot, and that the salt is a bed, not for eating.

Questions about how thoroughly the oysters are cooked, or who should avoid oysters, go to the service note and the kitchen. At Brennan's, a guest who wants oysters can be offered the Louisiana Oysters at breakfast and lunch, in a buttery, peppery New Orleans barbecue sauce, or at dinner the Grand Isle Jewel Oysters, served raw, with the raw shellfish advisory from the service note. Confirm at lineup how the Louisiana Oysters are cooked.

entries.title: Oysters Bienville
entries.summary: Baked oysters under a thick, rich sauce of shrimp, mushrooms, green onion and garlic, bound with roux and cream and enriched with yolk, finished with sherry, crumbs and cheese. Named for the founder of New Orleans, and claimed by two old houses.
entries.guest: Oysters Bienville are baked on the half shell under a creamy sauce of chopped shrimp, mushrooms and sherry, with a golden crust of breadcrumbs and cheese.

paras: Oysters Bienville is the other great baked oyster of the old New Orleans houses. Where Rockefeller is green and herbal, Bienville is ivory and rich: oysters on the half shell, each buried under a thick sauce of chopped shrimp, mushrooms, green onion and garlic, bound with a roux, flour cooked in butter, and milk or cream, enriched with egg yolk and sharpened with sherry, then crusted with breadcrumbs and cheese and baked until golden. The test for a cook is a sauce that stands on a hot oyster without running, yet eats creamy.

Shuck the oysters first, keep them chilled in their deep shells and strain their liquor, the salty juice from the shells. Sweat chopped green onion and garlic in butter without colour, add finely chopped mushrooms and cook until their water has gone, then stir in the flour and cook the roux for 2 to 3 minutes so it loses its raw taste. Whisk in warm, not hot, milk or cream a little at a time, with the oyster liquor, and simmer until very thick. Season with salt, white pepper and cayenne.

Off the heat, temper the yolks: whisk a ladle of hot sauce into them, then stir them back in. With this much roux the yolk is shielded, as it is in a pastry cream, so the sauce can come back to a gentle simmer for a minute; keep stirring so the thick sauce does not catch and scorch on the bottom. Then fold in the chopped cooked shrimp and a splash of dry sherry, so the shrimp only warm through and stay tender.

Spread the sauce in a tray, press cling film onto it and chill it firm, at least 2 hours. Pour off any liquor the oysters have given up since; some kitchens part-bake them for a minute and drain off the water that runs out. Nest the shells in hot rock salt, mound cold sauce over each oyster to the rim, and scatter it with breadcrumbs, grated Parmesan or Romano and a pinch of paprika. Bake at about 230°C (446°F) for 10 to 15 minutes, until bubbling and golden, with a moment under the salamander if it needs colour.

Take away the shrimp, mushrooms and sherry and what is left is a béchamel, milk thickened with a white roux, made about twice as thick as usual and enriched with yolk. That makes the Bienville sauce a New Orleans cousin in the béchamel family: a rich white sauce with a garnish, baked and browned like a gratin, a dish finished under a golden crust. Some kitchens use seafood stock and the oyster liquor in place of milk, which moves it towards velouté, a stock thickened with roux.

A sauce that floods the shell was too thin or went on warm: cook it thicker and chill it firm. A watery puddle under the crust comes from undrained oysters or mushrooms not cooked dry. A lumpy sauce had its liquid added too fast or too hot; shreds of cooked yolk mean the yolks went in untempered. A pasty, floury taste means the roux was not cooked out. A pale top needs a hotter oven or the salamander; a scorched top over a cold middle means the heat was too close. An oyster baked past the moment its edges curl turns small and tough.

The dish is named for Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne, Sieur de Bienville, the French officer, born in New France at what is now Montreal, who founded New Orleans in 1718 and governed the colony of Louisiana. Bienville Street in the French Quarter carries his name, and Arnaud's stands on it.

Who made it first is disputed. Arnaud's is the house most often linked with the dish, and some accounts credit its founder, Arnaud Cazenave. Antoine's claims it for its own kitchen, and other accounts say it began there and Arnaud's made it famous. No record settles it, so a server says that both houses claim it and picks no side.

Describe it plainly: oysters baked under a creamy sauce of chopped shrimp, mushrooms, green onion and sherry, with a golden crust of crumbs and cheese. Beside Rockefeller, it is the creamy one; Rockefeller is the green one. Say it BEE-en-vil. Warn the guest that the rock salt and shells are hot. Recipes vary from house to house, so any allergy or dietary question goes to the kitchen, never answered from memory.

entries.title: Shrimp rémoulade and Shrimp Arnaud
entries.summary: Chilled boiled Gulf shrimp dressed in a sharp Creole rémoulade on shredded lettuce, a starter of the old New Orleans houses. Shrimp Arnaud is Arnaud's own version, in its red rémoulade, and the house's signature starter.
entries.guest: Shrimp rémoulade is chilled Gulf shrimp in a tangy, peppery sauce of Creole mustard, paprika and horseradish, on crisp shredded lettuce.

paras: Shrimp rémoulade (REM-uh-lahd) is a cold starter: Gulf shrimp boiled in seasoned water, chilled hard, dressed in the New Orleans rémoulade and piled on shredded iceberg lettuce. It has long been a fixture of the old Creole houses, a cold, sharp opening before the rich dishes that follow. Shrimp Arnaud is Arnaud's own version: the same idea in the house's red rémoulade, and the starter the house is known for. For a cook the dish is two jobs done with care: shrimp cooked tender and chilled fast, and a sauce that is bright, hot and cold.

Cook the shrimp in a court-bouillon, a short, seasoned broth made for the purpose: water salted like the sea, about 30 g (1 oz) of salt to 1 litre (about 1 quart), with lemon, bay, onion, celery and cayenne or a crab boil seasoning, simmered for about 15 minutes to draw out the flavour. Bring it back to the boil, add the shrimp, shell on for more flavour, and let it return to a bare simmer.

Medium shrimp take 2 to 3 minutes: they are done when the flesh turns opaque and they curl into a loose C. A tight O means they went too long and will be tough. Some cooks cut the heat as the shrimp go in and let them steep for 3 to 5 minutes, which seasons them more and cooks them more gently.

Chill them fast. Lift the shrimp straight into an ice bath, roughly equal parts ice and water, salted a little so it does not wash out the seasoning, and leave them until cold right through. Fast chilling stops the cooking, keeps the flesh firm and moves the shrimp quickly through the warm temperatures in which bacteria grow. Drain them, peel and devein them, taking out the dark gut along the back, pat them dry and keep them covered at 5°C (41°F) or below. Wet shrimp water down the sauce.

Shred iceberg lettuce fine and keep it cold and dry. Toss the shrimp in the rémoulade close to service, or let them soak in it in the fridge if the house likes them that way; never dress the lettuce ahead, or it wilts. Pile the lettuce on a chilled plate, set the shrimp on top, spoon over a little more sauce and add a lemon wedge.

Every house makes its own rémoulade, and the versions fall into two camps. The red style is a dressing with no mayonnaise: Creole mustard, a coarse, vinegary whole-grain mustard, paprika, horseradish, lemon or vinegar and oil whisked together, brick red, sharp and hot, led by the mustard. The pink style is built on mayonnaise with the same seasonings stirred in, creamier and milder, led by the mayonnaise. Shrimp Arnaud belongs to the red camp. The first thing to learn on joining a kitchen is which camp the house is in. The sauce itself has its own entry.

Tough, rubbery shrimp curled into a tight O were overcooked: pull them at a loose C and chill them at once. Bland shrimp came from a liquor that was under-salted or not simmered before they went in. Soft, mushy shrimp were past their best, thawed in warm water or refrozen, or sat too long in a salty or acid dressing. A watery sauce and limp lettuce mean wet shrimp or lettuce dressed too early: dry everything and dress at the pass, the counter where plates leave the kitchen.

Describing the sauce is the server's job: tangy and peppery, coloured with paprika, sharp with Creole mustard, with the nose-tingling heat of horseradish and the crunch of finely chopped celery and green onion. Warn a guest who expects a mild, tartar-like sauce that this one has heat. Say the name REM-uh-lahd; RUM-uh-lahd is heard in New Orleans too.

Questions about egg in a pink rémoulade, about mustard or about shellfish go to the kitchen, never answered from memory. At Brennan's, a guest meets rémoulade as the chive rémoulade with the Crawfish Meat Pies, a snack on the Bubbles at Brennan's list in the Roost Bar and the courtyard; the menu does not print its recipe, so its style is a question for the kitchen too.

entries.title: Trout meunière and amandine at Galatoire's
entries.say: TROWT muhn-YEHR and ah-mahn-DEEN at GAL-uh-twahrz
entries.summary: Speckled trout, the Gulf's delicate spotted sea trout, floured and fried or sautéed, then covered with a dark New Orleans brown butter meunière and toasted almonds: Galatoire's trout meunière amandine, a classic of the Bourbon Street house.
entries.guest: At Galatoire's the trout comes floured and fried golden, under a dark, nutty brown butter sauce sharpened with lemon and scattered with toasted almonds.

paras: On the old New Orleans menus, trout means speckled trout, the spotted sea trout of the Gulf's bays and marshes. Despite the name it is no true trout: it belongs to the drum family, with redfish, and has soft, white, sweet flesh with a fine flake. The dish to know is the one Galatoire's made its own, trout meunière amandine: a fillet floured and fried or sautéed until golden, covered with a dark brown butter sauce, the meunière, and scattered with toasted sliced almonds. It joins two French ideas, à la meunière and amandine, on one plate.

Trim the fillets, skin off, and feel for pin bones, the fine bones along the centre line. Pat them dry and season them; just before they go in, dip them in milk or an egg wash, then dredge them in seasoned flour and shake off the excess; the flour browns into a golden crust and holds the delicate flesh together. Fry in oil at about 175°C (347°F), or sauté in clarified butter, butter with its milk solids removed, or oil in a hot pan for 2 to 3 minutes a side, turning once with a wide fish slice. Drain on a rack, never on paper, so the crust stays crisp.

Toast sliced almonds in a dry pan or a 160°C (320°F) oven for 5 to 8 minutes, until golden and fragrant; they burn quickly. For the meunière, cook butter over medium heat. It melts, foams as its water boils off, and its milk solids sink and brown. Take it past the hazelnut colour of the French beurre noisette to a deep brown with a strong, toasty smell, then pull it off the heat and add lemon juice, which hisses and spits, so stand back. Season it, add the almonds and spoon both over the fish at once.

The French à la meunière, the miller's wife's way, is lighter: the floured fish is cooked in butter, sprinkled with lemon juice and chopped parsley, and covered with foaming beurre noisette, butter browned only to a hazelnut gold. The New Orleans meunière goes darker and richer, browned further and sharpened with lemon, and in some houses built up with stock and seasonings into a fuller brown sauce. Each house keeps its own build, and Galatoire's has its own: teach the method, and describe the house's dish only as the house does. Amandine adds toasted almonds.

A soggy, greasy crust means oil that was too cool or a crowded pan. A coating that peels away means the fish was floured too long before cooking or turned before its crust had set. Butter taken past deep brown to black is bitter and cannot be saved: pour it out and start again. A fillet that breaks was handled roughly or turned more than once, and speckled trout forgives neither. Pale, soft almonds were not toasted long enough.

Galatoire's opened on Bourbon Street in 1905, founded by Jean Galatoire, and trout meunière amandine has long been one of its signature dishes. Trout Marguery, long a house speciality, is the other classic: trout under a rich, yolk-thickened sauce in the hollandaise family, with shrimp, named for sole Marguery, the dish of a Paris restaurant of that name. Together they show how the old menus dressed a delicate fish: meunière, amandine, Marguery, or crowned with lump crabmeat.

Ordering at Galatoire's has its own customs. For most of its history the downstairs dining room took no reservations, and on Fridays the line on Bourbon Street formed long before a lunch that runs well into the afternoon. The upstairs rooms now take reservations; how the downstairs room books today, Friday lunch included, is worth checking on the house's own site before you tell a guest. Regulars keep their own waiter for years and often order by asking what is good today.

Describe it as a delicate Gulf fish, floured and fried golden, under a dark, nutty brown butter with lemon and toasted almonds. Every nut or allergy question goes to the kitchen. At Brennan's, the nearest plate is the Pecan Gulf Fish at breakfast and lunch: the Gulf fish of the day topped with lump crab, with a pecan bordelaise; learn the day's fish, how it is cooked and which bordelaise it is at lineup.

entries.title: Pompano en papillote
entries.summary: Antoine's dish of pompano baked in a sealed paper parcel over a sauce of shrimp and crabmeat in a white wine velouté. The parcel puffs with steam in the oven and is cut open at the table.
entries.guest: Pompano en papillote is Antoine's classic: a rich Gulf fish baked in a paper parcel with shrimp and crab in a white wine sauce. Ours, the Gulf Fish en Papillote, uses banana leaf.

paras: Pompano en papillote, said POM-puh-noh ahn pah-pee-YOHT, is a fillet of pompano baked in a sealed paper parcel with a sauce of shrimp and crabmeat bound in a white wine velouté, a stock sauce thickened with a pale roux. In a hot oven the parcel swells with steam and reaches the table taut and browned at the edges, to be cut open before the guest in a rush of butter, wine and seafood.
It is one of the plates that made Antoine's famous.

Pompano here means the Florida pompano, a flat-sided, silvery fish of the jack family from the warm Gulf and south Atlantic. Its firm, white, rich flesh has a fine flake and enough natural fat to stay moist in a closed parcel. Fish of 450 g to 1.4 kg (1 to 3 lb) are usual, sold whole: look for bright eyes, red gills and a clean smell of the sea.

Make the sauce first and chill it, so it sits on the fish instead of running. Many classic recipes poach the fillets briefly in fish stock and white wine, then build the velouté from that liquid, so the oven has only to heat and puff the parcel. For four portions, cook 40 g (1.5 oz) each of butter and flour without colour, let the roux cool for a minute, then whisk in 500 ml (about 2 cups) of the hot liquid a ladle at a time and simmer 15 to 20 minutes, until it coats a spoon thickly.
Stir in a reduction of shallot and dry white wine, then 225 g (8 oz) each of cooked, chopped shrimp and lump crabmeat. Some cooks enrich it with a yolk off the heat. Season, then chill until set.

Butter a heart of baking parchment about 40 cm (16 inches) across for each portion. Spoon sauce onto one half, lay on a fillet of 150 to 180 g (5 to 6 oz), raw or lightly poached, and cover it with more sauce, then fold the paper over and crimp the edge tight; the entry on en papillote teaches the fold. Bake at 200 to 220°C (392 to 428°F) until the parcel puffs and browns: about 12 to 15 minutes for a raw fillet, 8 to 10 for one already poached, which needs only to heat through. The fish is done at 63°C (145°F) at its thickest point.

Inside the sealed paper, the sauce and the fish's juices turn to steam, which cooks the fish gently and inflates the parcel. Opening it at the table shows the guest the puff and releases the aroma with the fish at its moistest. Cut across the top and fold the edges away from the guest, so the steam rises clear of faces.

A parcel that leaks lets the steam out, so the paper never puffs and the fish dries: crimp tighter. A sauce that runs and scorches was too thin or not chilled. Because the paper hides the fish, overcooking is the commonest fault: cut fillets to one thickness and time each batch.

Antoine's credits Jules Alciatore, the founder's son, with the dish. The house story is that he created it for a dinner honouring Alberto Santos-Dumont, the Brazilian balloonist, and that the puffed paper recalled a balloon. Tellings usually place it around 1901, the year Santos-Dumont flew his airship round the Eiffel Tower and became famous across the world. Tell it as the house's story.

Our Gulf Fish en Papillote carries the idea forward: the day's Gulf fish wrapped in banana leaf rather than paper, with Louisiana crab, tomato, Castelvetrano olives, sorghum and Marcona almonds, so it steams in its own juices. The entry on en papillote teaches our dish in full. Learn the fish at lineup, and ask there whether the parcel is opened at the table.

When a guest mentions Antoine's pompano, link the two in a sentence: the same sealed parcel, another wrapper and another fish. Never call ours pompano unless lineup names it as the day's fish. Warn the guest that the steam is hot, and send questions about the shellfish or the almonds to the kitchen.

entries.title: Creole turtle soup
entries.say: As it reads: Creole turtle soup.
entries.summary: New Orleans' dark, thick turtle soup: turtle meat simmered with a brown roux, the trinity, tomato, stock and Worcestershire, finished with sherry, lemon and chopped hard-boiled egg. A Creole answer to the clear turtle soups of old banquets.
entries.guest: Creole turtle soup is a dark, rich soup of turtle meat, thickened with a brown roux and finished with sherry and egg. Ours is 100 per cent turtle meat, as the menu says.

paras: Creole turtle soup is a thick, dark brown soup of finely chopped turtle meat. A brown roux, flour cooked in fat until it smells of toasted nuts, gives body and a roasted depth; the trinity of onion, celery and green pepper, with garlic, tomato, stock, herbs and Worcestershire sauce, builds the flavour; and the turtle's gelatine gives a rich, lip-coating body. Dry sherry, lemon and chopped hard-boiled egg finish it, often with spinach or parsley.

For about 3 litres (about 3 quarts): 900 g (2 lb) turtle meat, a roux of 225 g (8 oz) each of fat and flour, 2 litres (about 2 quarts) of brown stock with 500 ml (about 2 cups) of the turtle cooking liquid, 400 g (14 oz) chopped tomato and 450 g (1 lb) of the trinity. A brown roux thickens less than a pale one, so a dark soup takes more of it.

Simmer the turtle meat in salted water with an onion and a bay leaf for 1 to 2 hours, until tender; chop it finely and keep the liquid. Cook a medium-brown roux in oil, lard or clarified butter in a heavy pot, stirring without stopping, for 25 to 35 minutes, until it is the colour of milk chocolate; the roux ladder teaches the stages. Add the trinity, which stops the browning, soften it for 5 to 8 minutes, then add the garlic.

Stir in the tomato, then add the stock and the turtle liquid, cool or barely warm, a ladle at a time, whisking so the roux takes it smoothly. Add the turtle, bay, thyme, Worcestershire and a little hot sauce, and keep it at a lazy simmer, 85 to 95°C (185 to 203°F), for 45 minutes to an hour, skimming the fat, until it coats a spoon. Off the heat, add lemon and sherry and season; scatter egg and parsley over each bowl. Hold it at 57°C (135°F) or above, the Food Code's hot holding figure.

Turtle soup was a banquet dish long before it was Creole. The green turtle soup of London's great City dinners was often served clear, as a consommé, a broth clarified until it is transparent, with Madeira or sherry, though thick versions were made too. Philadelphia's snapper soup, from freshwater snapping turtle, is thickened and served with sherry, a cousin of the Creole soup. New Orleans made its soup thick, dark and spiced as a rule.

Turtle was always dear, so cooks stretched it. Mock turtle soup, an English invention, uses calf's head for the same gelatinous body and holds no turtle at all. Many turtle soups still stretch the turtle with veal or beef, so a menu that prints 100 per cent turtle makes a real promise.

Black specks or an acrid smell in the roux mean it has scorched, and the whole pot will taste bitter: start again. A soup that tastes flat usually wants salt, lemon or sherry rather than more spice. Add the egg at the end: stirred in early, it breaks to crumbs and greys.

Turtle soup has been eaten in Louisiana since the 1700s, and the old houses each keep a famous version: Arnaud's, Commander's Palace, Mandina's and Brennan's among them. Commander's Palace is run by another branch of the Brennan family. Sea turtles are protected now, and New Orleans soups use freshwater snapping turtle.

Our Turtle Soup has its own entry. In short, the menu prints 100% turtle meat, finished with brown butter spinach, grated egg and aged sherry, and the turtle is snapping turtle; which kind, and who supplies it, are questions for the chef.

In many old dining rooms the server offers a splash of sherry from a cruet, a small pouring bottle, so each guest sets their own level. At Brennan's, whether the sherry goes in at the kitchen, at the pass, the counter where plates leave the kitchen, or at the table is a lineup question. Tell a guest avoiding alcohol that sherry is in the bowl, and never promise it cooks off. Describe the taste rather than the animal: rich, meaty and savoury, like a deep stew. If a guest eyes the courtyard fountain, smile and say it first: the soup is not the courtyard turtles, who are family. Allergen and dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

entries.title: Café brûlot
entries.summary: Burnt coffee: brandy and orange liqueur flamed in a bowl with sugar, cinnamon, cloves and orange and lemon peel, then hot coffee ladled in. A New Orleans tableside ritual credited to Antoine's, and the flavour behind our Café Brûlot Coffee Cake.
entries.guest: Café brûlot is New Orleans' flaming coffee: brandy, citrus peel and spice set alight, then hot coffee poured in. Our Café Brûlot Coffee Cake carries its coffee, citrus and spice.

paras: Café brûlot, said ka-FAY broo-LOH, means burnt coffee, from the French brûler, to burn. Brandy, usually with a little orange liqueur, is warmed in a wide bowl with sugar, cinnamon, cloves and strips of orange and lemon peel, then set alight. Once the spice and peel have scented the flaming spirit, hot, strong coffee is ladled in, the flame dies down, and the drink is served in small cups.

It matters because it is one of the city's great tableside rituals: an after-dinner coffee that is also a show, and part of the memory a guest takes home. At Brennan's it reaches the guest in another form, a coffee cake named for it, so a server needs to know both the drink and why the cake carries its name.

The brûlot set is a wide metal bowl, often silver, over a small burner, with a long-handled ladle and demitasse cups, the small cups used for strong coffee. For six to eight cups: 120 ml (4 fl oz) brandy, 30 ml (1 fl oz) orange liqueur, 25 g (2 tbsp) sugar or a few cubes, a cinnamon stick, 8 to 12 cloves, a strip of lemon peel, and an orange peeled in one long spiral and studded with cloves. Have 750 ml (about 3 cups) of hot, strong coffee ready before anything is lit.

With the burner still unlit, put the sugar, cinnamon, loose cloves and lemon peel in the bowl and add the brandy and orange liqueur, measured first in a small jug. Then light the burner low to warm them, and light the warm spirit with a long match, stirring gently to melt the sugar. Now the theatre: hold the clove-studded orange spiral up on a fork over the bowl, lift flaming brandy in the ladle and pour it slowly down the peel, so the flame runs along the spiral and draws the oil from the peel. Ladle the coffee in gradually until the flame dies, then ladle the drink into cups, leaving the spice and peel behind.
The rules for any flame at the table, from measuring the spirit before lighting to keeping a lid in reach, have their own entry, and so does tableside service.

Chicory coffee is the New Orleans base: roasted, ground chicory root blended with dark-roast coffee, which brings a roasty, gently bitter, chocolatey depth and a smooth body that stands up to brandy and spice. Brew it stronger than for an ordinary cup, because the spirit and sugar dilute it. Its cousins are the other warm, spirited coffees, such as Irish coffee, which add the spirit without the fire.

Spirit that will not light is too cold: warm it in the bowl first so its vapour can catch. A flame that leaps high means too much spirit or a bowl left too long on the burner; measure first and keep the heat low. A bitter drink comes from white pith left on the peel or coffee that boiled. A thin, sweet drink means the coffee was weak.

Tradition credits Antoine's, where Jules Alciatore, the founder's son, is said to have created café brûlot diabolique, the devilish version, in the late nineteenth century. The flaming bowl became a fixture of the long New Orleans dinner and has been served in several of the old houses, Arnaud's among them. At Brennan's today it is on no menu as a drink: the house carries its flavours in a cake instead. Tell the origin as tradition: like most famous drinks, its first night is not on record.

The drink itself is not on our current list. Brennan's borrows its flavours for the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake, a sweet starter at breakfast and lunch: a chicory coffee and bittersweet chocolate cake with pecans, a spiced citrus glaze and whipped crème fraîche. Sell it as the coffee's flavours, not the flame, and suggest a cup of our chicory coffee alongside.

If a guest asks for café brûlot, say plainly that the drink is not on today's menus and offer it only if the house confirms it. Offer instead the coffee cake named for it and a cup of our chicory coffee. Tell the story as Antoine's tradition, never as a Brennan's invention. Allergy and dietary questions about the cake, nuts included, go to the service note and the kitchen.

entries.title: Soufflé potatoes
entries.summary: Pommes soufflées: thin, even slices of potato fried twice, first in cooler oil to cook them, then in hot oil so they puff into hollow golden pillows. A classic of the old New Orleans houses, often served with béarnaise.
entries.guest: Soufflé potatoes are thin slices of potato fried twice, so they puff into crisp, hollow pillows. The old houses serve them with béarnaise for dipping.

paras: Soufflé potatoes, pommes soufflées in French, are thin slices of potato that puff in the fryer into crisp, golden, hollow pillows. They are fried twice: first in cooler oil to cook them through, then in very hot oil, where the water inside flashes to steam and blows the slice apart into two crisp skins with air between them. Salted and served at once, they are light and fragile.

They matter because they are a test. A slice cut unevenly, too thick or too thin, a potato carrying too much sugar or oil a few degrees too cool, and the slice stays flat. A cook who sends out a basket of evenly puffed soufflé potatoes has mastered slicing, oil temperature and timing at once, which is why chefs use them to judge a fry cook.

Choose a mature, floury potato such as a russet: high starch sets a firm skin, and low sugar stops it browning before it puffs. Potatoes kept in cold storage, below about 7°C (45°F), turn some starch to sugar, so avoid them. Square off the peeled potato and cut lengthwise slices about 3 mm (1/8 inch) thick on a mandoline, a flat slicer with an adjustable blade, every slice the same, then trim them to neat ovals. Some cooks rinse off the surface starch and others never wash the slices; every cook dries them thoroughly.

Two fryers run side by side. In the first, at about 150°C (302°F), fry the slices a few at a time for 4 to 6 minutes, keeping the oil moving over them, until they are cooked through, limp and blistered but not coloured. Lift them onto a rack. This stage is done ahead, and the cooled slices wait for service.

To order, drop them into the second fryer at 190 to 200°C (374 to 392°F). The good ones swell within seconds; fry them a minute or two more to crisp and colour, drain on a rack, salt and serve at once.

The first fry cooks the starch and dries each face into a thin skin while the centre stays moist. In the hot second fryer that moisture turns to steam faster than it can escape, the skins hold it, and the slice inflates. Any crack or thin spot lets the steam out.

Not every slice puffs, even in practised hands, so cooks fry more than they need and keep the flat ones off the plate. Flat slices were uneven, cracked, or cut too thick or too thin. Slices that brown before they puff come from a sugary potato or a first fry that ran too hot. Slices that puff and then collapse came out before the skins had crisped. A puffed slice softens within minutes, so they are fried to order and carried straight out.

The legend says they were found by accident in France on the day in 1837 when the railway from Paris to Saint-Germain-en-Laye opened. The royal party was late, so the chef, Collinet, pulled his half-fried potatoes from the oil; when the guests arrived he plunged them back into hot oil and they puffed. The details change with the teller, from who was late to the year, so tell it as legend. The same tradition credits Collinet with béarnaise.
New Orleans kept them. Antoine's, Arnaud's and Galatoire's have long served soufflé potatoes, often with béarnaise for dipping, and guests order them to taste the old city.

Soufflé potatoes are not on Brennan's current menus, so a guest who asks hears the story. One who wants crisp fried potatoes can be offered the Brabant Potatoes (bra-BAHNT), a breakfast and lunch side of cubed potatoes fried golden and tossed in butter with garlic and parsley; confirm the house finish at lineup. Wherever soufflé potatoes are served, they go to the table the moment they leave the fryer, with the béarnaise beside them. Warn the guest that the first bite lets out hot steam.

entries.title: Bread pudding soufflé
entries.summary: Commander's Palace's signature: New Orleans bread pudding folded into meringue and baked tall in a ramekin, with whiskey sauce poured into its centre at the table. It marries a set bread custard to a soufflé, and Brennan's does not serve it.
entries.guest: The bread pudding soufflé is the famous dessert of Commander's Palace, run by another branch of the Brennan family. Ours is the New Orleans Bread Pudding, with whiskey caramel and pralines.

paras: A bread pudding soufflé is New Orleans bread pudding broken up, folded through whipped egg white and baked in a ramekin, a small straight-sided dish, until it rises tall above the rim. It is the signature dessert of Commander's Palace in the Garden District, where the server opens the top at the table and pours whiskey sauce into the centre. Guests ask for it by name at the wrong house.

It marries two techniques. Bread pudding is a set bread custard: bread soaked in sweet custard and baked until the egg sets. A soufflé, French for puffed, is a flavoured base lightened with meringue, egg white whipped with sugar; here the broken pudding is the base. In the oven the air expands, water turns to steam and the egg white sets round the bubbles. The pudding brings flavour and body; the meringue brings lift.

Bake the bread pudding first: cubes of light New Orleans French bread soaked in eggs, cream, sugar, vanilla and spice, baked at 180°C (356°F) for 30 to 40 minutes in a shallow pan, until set at the centre, about 80°C (176°F) on a probe. Cool it completely, because a warm, wet pudding melts the meringue and sinks the rise.

Brush the ramekins with soft butter in upward strokes and coat them with sugar: the soufflé climbs the walls on that grip. In a spotless bowl with no trace of yolk or fat, whip the whites with a pinch of cream of tartar, a powdered acid that steadies the foam, adding the sugar a spoonful at a time, to firm, glossy peaks that bend slightly at the tip, never dry and grainy.

Break the cold pudding into small pieces and stir in a quarter of the meringue to loosen it. Fold in the rest in two additions: cut down through the middle with a large spatula, sweep along the bottom and up the side, turn the bowl and repeat, stopping once the white streaks are gone. Fill the ramekins to the rim, wipe the rims and run a thumb round the inside edge so the top rises straight. Bake at 180°C (356°F) for 15 to 20 minutes, the door shut for the first ten.

It is ready with straight sides, a rise of about 2.5 cm (1 inch) above the rim, a golden top and a gentle wobble when nudged. It falls as it cools, so it goes straight to the table. Many restaurant versions thicken cream with cornflour (cornstarch) mixed smooth in cold water, a slurry, then sweeten it and finish it with bourbon; the older New Orleans whiskey sauce is butter, sugar and egg.

A flat, dense soufflé means underwhipped meringue, heavy folding or a trace of fat in the bowl. A lopsided rise comes from patchy butter, mix on the rim or a hot spot in the oven. A grainy meringue that weeps beads of syrup had its sugar added too fast or was whipped past glossy. A wet layer at the bottom means the pudding was underbaked or still warm. One that sinks before the table was underbaked or waited at the pass, the counter where plates leave the kitchen: fire it to the guest's pace.

Brennan's does not serve a bread pudding soufflé. Its dessert is the New Orleans Bread Pudding: bread pudding with a warm whiskey caramel, buttermilk ice cream for tang and pralines for crunch. Mention the whiskey to a guest who avoids alcohol.

Guests mix the houses up because both carry the Brennan name. Owen Brennan opened in 1946, and the restaurant has been at 417 Royal Street since 1956. The family split in 1973, settled in 1974: Owen's widow and sons kept Royal Street, and Ella Brennan's side took Commander's Palace. Brennan's closed in 2013 and reopened in November 2014 under Ralph Brennan, a cousin, and his partner Terry White; the two houses are separate businesses.

When a guest asks for the bread pudding soufflé, never correct them sharply; it is an easy mistake. Say it is the famous dessert at Commander's Palace, run by another branch of the Brennan family, and offer ours. Allergy and dietary questions about any dessert go to the service note and the kitchen.

entries.title: Crêpes Suzette at the table
entries.summary: Thin crêpes warmed in beurre Suzette, a sauce of butter, sugar and orange, then flamed with orange liqueur and brandy. A founding flamed dessert whose origin is told in rival stories, still made at the table in the old New Orleans houses.
entries.guest: Crêpes Suzette are thin French pancakes warmed in butter, sugar and orange, then flamed with orange liqueur and brandy. Our flamed dessert is the Bananas Foster, made at your table.

paras: Crêpes Suzette are thin French pancakes warmed in beurre Suzette, a sauce of butter, sugar and orange juice and zest, then flamed with orange liqueur and brandy and served in their syrup. A crêpe (KRAYP) is a pancake of thin batter with no raising agent, cooked fast in a hot pan until supple and lacy. Still made at the table in the old New Orleans houses, it asks for three skills: thin crêpes, a glossy citrus syrup and a calm flame.

Whisk 125 g (1 cup) flour, a pinch of salt and a spoonful of sugar with 2 eggs, then whisk in 300 ml (1 1/4 cups) milk a little at a time, against lumps, and finish with 30 g (1 oz) melted butter. It should pour like thin cream. Rest it, covered and chilled, for at least an hour: the flour absorbs the liquid and the bubbles settle, so the crêpes come out thin and tender.

Heat an 18 to 20 cm (7 to 8 inch) crêpe pan over a medium-high flame and wipe it with clarified butter. Pour in about 45 ml (3 tbsp) of batter and tilt and swirl at once into a thin sheet. After about a minute the edges turn lacy and lift; turn it and give the second side 20 to 30 seconds. Allow three a guest.

For the sauce, melt butter and sugar in a wide pan until pale gold, add orange juice and zest, often with a little lemon, and reduce to a glossy syrup. Coat each crêpe on both sides, fold it into quarters with the prettier first-cooked side outward, and push it aside. Off the flame add orange liqueur, such as Grand Marnier, and brandy, usually Cognac; return the pan, tilt to light it, spoon the burning syrup over, and plate once the flame dies.

Crêpes Suzette heads a small family of flamed desserts. Cherries jubilee is generally credited to Escoffier for one of Queen Victoria's jubilees, most often said to be 1897: cherries in a thickened syrup, lit with kirsch, a clear cherry brandy. Bananas Foster, created at Brennan's in 1951, flames bananas in a caramel of butter, brown sugar and cinnamon with rum, and banana liqueur in the house's published recipe. Each is a hot syrup, a warmed spirit and a flame.

Thick, rubbery crêpes mean a batter too thick or unrested, or too much in the pan. Tears on turning mean a cool pan or a crêpe turned too soon. A bitter sauce had its sugar taken too dark, or pith came with the zest. A greasy, separated sauce boiled too hard: swirl in orange juice off the heat. Soggy crêpes sat too long in the syrup.

Nobody knows who first made it, so tell the stories as stories. The best known is Henri Charpentier's: in his memoir he said that in 1895, as an assistant waiter at the Café de Paris in Monte Carlo, he lit the sauce by accident while serving the Prince of Wales, later Edward VII, who named it for a young lady at his table, Suzette. Charpentier was then a teenager, and the Larousse Gastronomique doubts that a boy so young served a prince. Another story names a Paris actress known as Suzette who served crêpes on stage.

Escoffier's Guide Culinaire, in its 1907 English edition, A Guide to Modern Cookery, warms the crêpes in a butter of mandarin zest and juice, sugar and curaçao, an orange liqueur, with no flame at all: the flame came later, as tableside theatre. In New Orleans the old houses, Arnaud's among them, have long made crêpes Suzette at the table; menus change, so check a house's current menu before telling a guest it is served.

Crêpes Suzette is not on the Brennan's menu, but its family is. The World Famous Bananas Foster, created by the house in 1951, is flamed at the table on the guéridon, the tableside cart. Cherries Jubilee is flamed the same way, but it is not on the dessert menu of 3 October 2026: confirm with a manager that it is served before offering it.

A guest who asks for crêpes Suzette here wants flame, orange and a little theatre: offer the Foster in the same terms. Flaming burns off some of the alcohol, never all, so say so to a guest who avoids alcohol. Say it KRAYP soo-ZET; KREP, nearer the French, is also heard.
